v.why: Near-divergent learning rates are partly stabilized by lower-noise larger-batch gradients, while update count is no longer the bottleneck.
With Adam a fixed per-parameter step moves wider nets' outputs further, so width compensates for too-small learning rates.
Narrow nets are already capacity-limited and do not overfit, so extra weight shrinkage pushes them into underfitting more than wide nets.
Gradient and update magnitudes compound across layers, so deeper ReLU stacks diverge or die more readily at large learning rates.
Small batches supply many updates within 243 epochs, letting deeper nets actually realize their extra capacity.
Single-hidden-layer nets get capacity only from width, whereas deeper nets already have enough representational power.
Stacking narrow ReLU layers creates information bottlenecks and dead units that make the extra layer harmful rather than helpful.
Large batches give few, low-noise updates per epoch, so a larger step size is needed to converge within the budget.
Heavy L2 forces the net into an underfit regime where extra units are shrunk toward zero and add little, unlike at mild regularization where width helps.
Tiny batches give many noisy updates, so lowering the learning rate reduces noise at little cost in convergence.
